items.text:
No show/last minute (<24 hour) cancellations... how do you deal with them?

We have a policy in our financial agreement, with a place to be individually initialed by the patient (so that it stands out), of $100/scheduled hour for no-show or cancel with <24 hours notice... rarely enforced (probably should be more so).

Full mouth reconstruction case scheduled over 2 days, no other patients scheduled those days... $30k... patient canceled 5 minutes before 1st appointment... ultimately rescheduled.  Applied $800 fee to his account and he blew a gasket...

What would you do?  Ultimately, I waived the fee even though there is a history of this behavior but $30k vs $800 is pretty much a no brainer.

topComments.text:
For a case like that you should get half the money upfront before treatment. 
Charging an $800 no show fee is a good way to lose a a big case and a patient.
Maybe you can add the $800 in estimate and say if you don’t cancel any appointments last minute and no show then we will give you $800 discount at the end of the Tx

items.text:
Hi everyone! I could really use some advice from dental office managers/front desk teams

I work in a small private dental office, and I currently handle a little of everything, dental billing, insurance verification, treatment coordination, reception, claims, denials, AR, etc.

The  office is growing, and I need to 
 Focus  more toward managing the office and training staff, so my doctor and I are looking into hiring someone who can take ownership of billing and insurance responsibilities.

We’re thinking about someone who could handle things like:
• Insurance verification & breakdowns
• Claims and follow-ups
• Denials and appeals
• EOBs and insurance payments
• AR / outstanding balances
• Treatment estimates and insurance coordination

For those of you working in small private practices, how have you structured this? Did you hire a dedicated dental biller/insurance coordinator, outsource billing, or have someone work remotely?

Any advice on what position/title to look for, what responsibilities to include, and how you got started would be greatly appreciated! Thank you! 🙏🏻

topComments.text:
I work with a relatively new private practice that has grown tremendously over the last year. The doctor initially hired one front desk person, but as the practice grew, she needed some additional support on the billing/insurance side.

I handle their billing remotely, including insurance verification, claim submission, appeals, insurance aging and follow-up, payment posting, and patient AR. I’ve also helped with fee negotiations, and because I handle the payment posting, I’m able to keep track of what fee schedules and contracted rates everything is being paid under.

For patient AR, I created a spreadsheet that works well for her to keep track of outstanding balances and follow-ups.

Having someone take ownership of that side of things has allowed her to focus much more on the day-to-day operations of the practice and, most importantly, patient care. We work closely throughout the day, and she’s able to message me anytime she has a question or needs something looked into.

I mention this just because a remote setup like this is definitely an option and can work really well for a growing practice🙂
Where are you located. Have you ever thought about outsourcing this. Unfortunately Treatment est would be difficult, but there are ways around it.

items.text: Hello, does anyone know good reps to go through for Listerine? thank you in advance! ￼

Thank you to everyone who offered ways for me to try to get through to a rep at MetLife. I spent most of my afternoon trying the different ways and to no avail. We are OON with them and we are DONE! As of 2027 we will no longer take assignment of benefits. We will bill the claim, but patients will pay up front and MetTrash can reimburse them. This will be the first time doing this with any insurance. What is the best way to let our patients know and what is the most profesional wording to use? We don’t want to lose patients over this, but the issues we are having with them isn’t worth the stress.

topComments.text: I’d send an email or letter now and remind patients when scheduling. Something like: “Beginning January 1, 2027, we’ll continue to accept MetLife patients and submit claims on your behalf. Payment will be due at your visit, and MetLife will send any eligible reimbursement directly to you. We’re happy to review your estimated cost before your appointment.”

This is what you should be doing with all out of network insurance. We are an oon office and that is how we do it.  No ridiculous A/R, no wasting time on insurance verifications and zero sitting on hold waiting to get through to insurance companies. We file a claim as a courtesy.  You should send a blanket letter saying that as of 1/1/27, any oon insurance will be  ffs. Assign all oon to go to the patient. You will be so happy you did this.
